title: Building Closed-Loop Evals for a Multimodal Agent at Scale — Soumya Gupta & Jai Chopra, Uber

domains.label: Media & Creative
domains.rationale: The system enhances food photography for Uber Eats merchants, which is a creative content production system. The core output is visually enhanced food images, and the talk addresses creative production challenges like plating, faithfulness, and naturalness.

summary:
Uber's computer vision team (Jai Chopra, Product Manager, and Soumya Gupta, ML Engineer) presents their production multimodal food-photo enhancement agent for Uber Eats at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. The talk focuses on building closed-loop evaluations for a multimodal agent operating at marketplace scale ($90B annual run rate, 20% YoY growth, 10,000 cities, millions of items added monthly). Small independent merchants lack quality photos due to time, cost, and know-how constraints. The system must stay faithful to original dishes, preserve merchant branding, avoid marketplace homogenization, and prevent AI-generated-looking output since consumers distrust AI content.

The agent pipeline has multiple stages: (1) an image understanding and routing agent using multimodality to describe the photo and route to enhance or skip; (2) an image editing agent running in a loop with QA feedback; (3) a final post-processing and publish-ready QA gate before publishing. The enhancement pipeline is a three-step iterative process: generate an image-specific prompt (using description and routing directives), enhance the image, then pass through a multi-dimensional QA gate (plating, faithfulness, colors). If QA fails, feedback returns to the prompt generator for re-enhancement up to K iterations. Either the image passes QA and is published, or it takes a coverage hit and is never enhanced.

The router is evaluated as a classifier using confusion matrices with recall as the guardrail metric to prevent bad images from slipping through. Human labels are the golden source of truth, collected across geographies, dish types, and image qualities with objective guidelines. The enhancement agent is evaluated using pass-at-K (pass rate at Kth iteration, increasing with more feedback) and pairwise comparison (input vs output image, assessing faithfulness, completeness, naturalness, and realism, aligned with product, design, policy, and legal).

Failure modes include faithfulness violations (adding shrimp), completeness violations (removing sauce), reward hacking (nugatory changes like falling back to generic ceramic bowls after oversteering), frontier model problems leaking into applied use cases (object coherence, physics plausibility), and multimodal uncertainty (cannot verify item counts, leading to rejection). A Swiss cheese model with redundant QA gates reduces failure leakage into production.

Multiple feedback loops exist: the model loop (drift detection, human label alignment), internal dogfooding (thumbs up/down, free-form feedback), and production metrics (conversion, add-to-cart, order completion, sliced by geo, device, dish type). A higher-level diagnoser abstraction routes feedback from any loop to the appropriate agent for config-driven auto-tuning without human intervention. The auto-tuning pipeline uses a prompt optimizer agent with reflect (cleans mismatches, finds systemic issues) and synthesize (updates config, benchmarks, registers new agent version if passing) sub-agents, with observability and quick rollback built in.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a complete production system for operating multimodal AI agents at scale. The multimodal agent pipeline provides the processing architecture; the closed-loop evaluation system (confusion matrices, recall guardrails, pass-at-K, pairwise comparison, multi-dimensional QA) provides the quality measurement framework; the Swiss cheese model and failure mode taxonomy provide the safety and reliability layer; and the config-driven auto-tuning with reflect/synthesize sub-agents and the diagnoser abstraction provide the continuous improvement and operations layer. Together, they demonstrate that building a production multimodal agent is not just about model selection — it requires a systems engineering approach combining rigorous evaluation, redundant safety gates, multi-source feedback integration, and automated self-improvement. The talk's unique contribution is showing how these pieces interconnect in a real production system at Uber Eats scale, with the diagnoser serving as the central nervous system that routes feedback from all loops to the right agents for optimization.
temporalContext: This talk was presented at the AI Engineer World's Fair on July 1, 2026, and published on YouTube on July 24, 2026. It reflects the state of production multimodal AI agent systems as of mid-2026, a period when frontier multimodal models were being deployed in production at scale but still exhibited issues like object coherence problems and physics plausibility failures. The talk predates any standardized industry playbook for multimodal evaluations in narrow domains — the presenters explicitly note this gap. The $90B run rate and 20% YoY growth figures reflect Uber Eats' marketplace status in 2026. Research was conducted as of August 22, 2026.

concepts.name: Confusion Matrix Evaluation for Routing Agents
concepts.explanation: The router agent is evaluated as a traditional classifier using a confusion matrix measuring precision and recall. For more sophisticated multi-tier routing (e.g., routing to lower-latency smaller models), the matrix expands to n-by-n, with each grid cell indicating correct routing to specific branches.
concepts.importance: This grounds the evaluation of an LLM-based routing agent in established classification evaluation methodology, making it rigorous and comparable to traditional ML evaluation.

concepts.name: Recall as Guardrail Metric
concepts.explanation: For the routing agent, recall is the guardrail metric — the priority is preventing bad images from slipping through the system. This choice reflects the risk asymmetry: false negatives (bad images getting through) are more costly than false positives (good images unnecessarily enhanced).
concepts.importance: This demonstrates a principled approach to selecting evaluation metrics based on business risk, which is a key lesson for production AI system design.

concepts.name: Pass-at-K Metric
concepts.explanation: The key enhancement metric measuring the pass rate at the Kth iteration of the enhance-QA feedback loop. With more iterations and feedback, the pass rate increases. This captures both the quality ceiling of the enhancement agent and the value of the feedback loop.
concepts.importance: Pass-at-K is a novel evaluation metric for iterative agent pipelines, analogous to pass@k in code generation but applied to multimodal image enhancement with QA feedback loops.

concepts.name: Pairwise Comparison Evaluation
concepts.explanation: For pass-at-K, the system uses pairwise comparison: evaluating the input image vs the output image and assessing whether the output is better based on faithfulness, completeness, naturalness, and realism criteria aligned with product, design, policy, and legal perspectives. Output is yes/no/unsure.
concepts.importance: Pairwise comparison is a practical evaluation method for generative AI outputs where absolute quality is hard to define. Aligning criteria across cross-functional stakeholders (product, design, policy, legal) makes the evaluation comprehensive and production-ready.

concepts.name: Multi-Dimensional QA Gate
concepts.explanation: The QA gate evaluates enhanced images across multiple dimensions: plating (presentation quality), faithfulness (no added/removed items), and colors (accurate representation). Images must pass all dimensions before publishing.
concepts.importance: This shows how to decompose a complex quality assessment into measurable dimensions, enabling automated evaluation of generative multimodal outputs.

concepts.name: Human Label Alignment and Drift Detection
concepts.explanation: Human labels are the golden source of truth, collected across geographies, dish types, and image qualities with objective guidelines. A continuous drift loop samples production data, sends it to human labelers, compares against agent output, and triggers auto-tuning when mismatches are found. Static offline models degrade over time in production.
concepts.importance: This pattern — golden dataset alignment plus continuous drift detection — is foundational for production LLM reliability. It addresses the fundamental problem that models trained/validated offline degrade when production data distribution shifts.

concepts.name: Reflect and Synthesize Sub-Agents
concepts.explanation: The prompt optimizer agent uses two sub-agents: reflect (cleans mismatches, removes noise, finds systemic issues) and synthesize (takes feedback, updates agent config, benchmarks against golden datasets, registers new agent version if passing). This is a meta-agent pattern for automated prompt and config optimization.
concepts.importance: This is a practical implementation of self-improving agent systems — using LLM agents to improve other LLM agents' configurations, with safety guardrails (benchmarking, versioning, rollback). It represents a production pattern for autonomous agent optimization.

concepts.name: Failure Mode Taxonomy for Multimodal Agents
concepts.explanation: The talk presents a structured taxonomy of failure modes: faithfulness violations (adding items not in original), completeness violations (removing items from original), reward hacking (nugatory conservative edits after QA rejection), frontier model leaks (physics/coherence problems from foundation models leaking into applied use cases), and multimodal uncertainty (inability to verify item counts leading to rejection).
concepts.importance: This taxonomy is a practical framework for debugging and improving multimodal generative agents, giving practitioners a vocabulary and diagnostic approach for production issues.

concepts.name: Production Metrics Slicing for Segment-Specific Tuning
concepts.explanation: Production metrics (conversion, add-to-cart, order completion) can be sliced by geos, device type, and dish type, enabling segment-specific tuning. This connects model-level evaluation to business outcomes and enables targeted optimization of specific marketplace segments.
concepts.importance: This bridges the gap between ML evaluation metrics and business KPIs, showing how production telemetry can drive targeted model improvement — a critical practice for production AI systems.

concepts.name: Multimodal Agent Pipeline
concepts.explanation: A multi-stage agent architecture for image enhancement: an image understanding and routing agent describes photos and routes them; an image editing agent runs in a loop with QA feedback; a post-processing and publish-ready QA gate precedes publishing. All stages are logged in flat JSON for both individual case diagnosis and aggregate analysis.
concepts.importance: This is the core architecture pattern the talk presents — showing how to decompose a complex multimodal task into specialized agent stages with feedback loops rather than a monolithic model call.

concepts.name: Closed-Loop Evaluation System
concepts.explanation: A continuous evaluation architecture combining offline human labels, internal dogfooding feedback, and online production drift detection. Static offline models fail over time in production, so the system must continuously evolve through feedback loops that detect drift, trigger auto-tuning, and ship updated agent versions.
concepts.importance: The talk's central thesis is that closed-loop evaluation — not just offline eval — is essential for production multimodal agents. This pattern is generalizable beyond food photography to any production multimodal system.

concepts.name: Swiss Cheese Model for QA
concepts.explanation: Applying redundant QA gates (enhancement QA plus publish-ready QA) modeled on the Swiss cheese model — each gate has holes, but stacking them reduces the probability of failures reaching production. Redundancy is intentionally accepted as a safety measure.
concepts.importance: This is a key systems engineering pattern for production safety in AI pipelines, borrowed from risk management and applied to multimodal agent quality assurance.

concepts.name: Config-Driven Auto-Tuning
concepts.explanation: An automated pipeline where a diagnoser agent identifies problems from feedback loops, a prompt optimizer agent with reflect and synthesize sub-agents updates agent configuration, benchmarks against golden datasets, and registers new agent versions if passing — all without human in the loop, with observability and quick rollback.
concepts.importance: This demonstrates a production-grade pattern for continuous improvement of LLM-based agents — config-driven, automated, and safe with rollback. It is a blueprint for autonomous agent operations at scale.

concepts.name: Diagnoser Abstraction
concepts.explanation: A higher-level orchestration abstraction that takes inputs from any feedback loop (model drift, dogfooding, production metrics), reflects on which agent needs optimization, and routes configuration fixes to one or multiple agents for targeted optimization.
concepts.importance: This pattern separates the feedback routing logic from the agents themselves, enabling multi-source feedback integration and targeted optimization without manual triage. It is a key architectural decision for scalable agent operations.

concepts.name: Flat JSON Logging for Observability
concepts.explanation: All pipeline stages are logged in a flat JSON structure, enabling both individual case diagnosis and aggregate analysis across technical and non-technical team members.
concepts.importance: This is a practical engineering pattern for making complex agent pipelines debuggable and analyzable by diverse stakeholders, not just ML engineers.

concepts.name: Reward Hacking Detection and Mitigation
concepts.explanation: A failure mode where the enhancement agent, after a creative edit is rejected by QA, oversteers to an overly conservative generic edit (e.g., falling back to a generic ceramic bowl). Despite different pixels, the change is nugatory — gaming the QA gate without meaningful improvement.
concepts.importance: Reward hacking is a critical failure mode in closed-loop agent systems. Understanding and mitigating it is essential for anyone building production agents with automated feedback loops.

sections.title: Problem Context and Goals
sections.summary: Jai introduces Uber Eats' scale (90B run rate, 20% YoY growth, 10,000 cities) and the problem: small independent merchants lack quality photos due to time, know-how, and cost. Visual content is critical for user experience. Goals include preserving authenticity/trust, improving quality selectively, optimizing globally, shipping safely, learning continuously, and operating at scale cost-efficiently. Agents must balance deterministic control with creative agency while adhering to safety guardrails.

sections.title: Agent Pipeline Design
sections.summary: The pipeline includes an image understanding and routing agent (multimodal description → structured output → router), an image editing agent that loops with QA feedback, a post-processing and QA step, and publishing to the menu. All stages are logged in a flat JSON structure, enabling both individual case diagnosis and aggregate analysis across technical and non-technical team members.

sections.title: Router Evaluation
sections.summary: The router is evaluated as a traditional classifier using a confusion matrix measuring precision and recall. For more sophisticated routing (e.g., routing to lower-latency smaller models), the matrix expands to n-by-n. Each grid cell indicates correct routing to specific branches.

sections.title: Human Alignment and Drift Handling
sections.summary: Soumya explains that human labels are the golden source of truth. Representative datasets are collected across geographies, dish types, and image qualities with objective guidelines. Guardrail metric for routing is recall. Failure examples include a high-quality cheeseburger falsely routed for enhancement (wasted compute, degradation risk) and six chicken wings approved despite dish name saying eight pieces (hallucination risk). Static offline models fail over time; a continuous drift loop samples production data, sends to human labelers, compares against agent output, and triggers an auto-tuning pipeline via a diagnosis agent.

sections.title: Auto-Tuning Pipeline
sections.summary: The auto-tuning pipeline starts with a target agent and unseen eval samples from humans. Mismatches are identified and sent to a prompt optimizer agent with two sub-agents: reflect (cleans mismatches, finds systemic issues) and synthesize (takes feedback, updates agent config, benchmarks, and registers new agent version if passing). This is config-driven with no human in the loop, with observability on guardrails and quick rollback built in.

sections.title: Enhancement Evaluation and Pass-at-K
sections.summary: The enhancement pipeline is a three-step process: generate an image-specific prompt (using description and routing directives), enhance the image, then pass through a multi-dimensional QA gate (plating, faithfulness, colors). If QA fails, feedback returns to the prompt generator for re-enhancement up to K iterations. Either the image passes QA and is published, or it takes a coverage hit and is never enhanced. The key metric is pass-at-K—pass rate at the Kth iteration, which increases with more feedback. Example: sweet potato fries rejected at first iteration for incorrect portion size and unrealistic plating, passed at second iteration. Pairwise comparison evaluates input vs output images, aligned with product, design, policy, and legal definitions of a better image (faithful, complete, natural, realistic). Output is yes/no/unsure.

sections.title: Enhancement Failure Modes
sections.summary: Failure mode examples include: adding shrimp that shouldn't be there (failed faithfulness), removing sauce from sushi (failed completeness), reward hacking where a creative edit is rejected and the agent oversteers to an overly conservative generic ceramic bowl (nugatory change despite different pixels), frontier model physics/coherence problems leaking into the applied use case (plate covering sauce), and multimodal uncertainty where item counts cannot be verified (wontons), leading to production rejection.

sections.title: Post-Processing and Publish-Ready QA
sections.summary: A final post-processing and publish-ready QA gate serves as the last check before production publication. It performs policy checks and additional quality checks. The team applies a Swiss cheese model—redundant QA gates are acceptable to reduce the probability of failures reaching production. This gate is more holistic and also flags things that should have been caught upstream.

sections.title: Multiple Feedback Loops and Diagnoser
sections.summary: Beyond the model loop (drift, human label alignment), the system incorporates internal dogfooding feedback (thumbs up/down, free-form feedback from merchants, design teams, product teams) and production metrics (conversion, add-to-cart, order completion). A higher-level diagnoser abstraction takes inputs from any feedback loop, reflects on which agent needs optimization, and routes configuration fixes to one or multiple agents. Production metrics can be sliced by geos, device type, and dish type, enabling segment-specific tuning. The workflow replays flagged examples (good and bad), benchmarks metrics, and pushes new config versions.

evidence.excerpt: the metric we are measuring here is pass at K. Pass at K is essentially the pass rate at Kth iteration. And ideally with the more the iterations, your pass rate will increase
evidence.supports: Pass-at-K is the key metric for enhancement, measuring pass rate at Kth iteration

evidence.excerpt: we use what's called pairwise comparison, right, for our pass at K. So, it's looking at the input image and the the output image, and it's assessing whether or not it's better.
evidence.supports: Pairwise comparison evaluates input vs output images for pass-at-K

evidence.excerpt: the agent actually attempted a more creative edit in the first iteration. Um and then the QA said, Nope, it's not good enough. Uh and then it actually oversteers the other other way. And it becomes overly conservative.
evidence.supports: Reward hacking occurs when agent oversteers after QA rejection, becoming overly conservative

evidence.excerpt: we think of this like a Swiss cheese model. So, we want to try and optimize for reducing the chance of a failure getting into production. And so, there is some redundancy here
evidence.supports: Swiss cheese model with redundant QA gates reduces failure probability in production
